title: Three hours of worsening breathlessness a month after a heart attack
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of Sam Stevens, a 73-year-old man in a metropolitan ED with 2 weeks of worsening breathlessness that became much worse over the last 3 hours. He had a heart attack a month ago, has poorly controlled hypertension and has been taking a lot of over-the-counter ibuprofen for back pain. The candidate then interprets his observations, ECG, bloods with a venous gas and chest X-ray, diagnoses acute pulmonary oedema from heart failure brought on by the recent MI and the NSAID use, outlines ED management and safety-nets.
focus: Acute breathlessness after a recent MI: eliciting heart failure symptoms and the NSAID precipitant, reading a chest X-ray of pulmonary oedema systematically, and managing acute pulmonary oedema in the ED
diagnosis: Congestive heart failure after recent myocardial infarction
stem: You are the intern in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital. Sam Stevens, a 73-year-old man, has come in with shortness of breath. His wife drove him in. He is sitting up on a trolley in an acute bay, on a cardiac monitor, with an IV cannula in place. A nurse is with you and can carry out your instructions. The nurse has recorded an ECG and sent bloods with a venous blood gas, and a portable chest X-ray has been requested. The ED consultant has asked you to assess him.
tasks: Take a focused history from Sam and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. He is very breathless, so keep your questions targeted (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you his observations, ECG, blood results with a venous gas, and chest X-ray report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Sam Stevens, a 73-year-old retired man. You are not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin. You are sitting bolt upright, breathing fast, sweaty, and you cannot finish a sentence without stopping for breath. Every so often you cough into a tissue. You are frightened but you want to cooperate. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they examine.

What the nurse reports at the start (when the candidate asks, or straight away if they do not): "Sam's wife brought him in about 15 minutes ago. The triage set on room air at 10:42 was resp rate 32, sats 87%, heart rate 108 and regular, BP 206 over 108, temp 36.8, BGL 7.2. The repeat at 10:50 on room air was resp rate 34, sats 86%, heart rate 114, BP 212 over 112. He's on the monitor, the cannula is in, bloods and a venous gas have gone, the ECG is done and the portable X-ray is on its way. I'm getting the oxygen ready. What would you like?"

How you change with what the candidate does:

  • If they ask for oxygen, the nurse asks: "What saturation are you aiming for?" With oxygen your sats rise to about 92%, but you are still very breathless.
  • If they keep you sitting upright, say: "Don't lie me down, I can't breathe flat."
  • If they ask for GTN (under the tongue or a drip), after a few minutes you breathe a little more easily. Your BP comes down to about 160/90 and your heart rate to about 104.
  • If they ask for CPAP or non-invasive ventilation, the nurse says the machine is being set up and the senior ED doctor is coming.
  • If they call the senior ED doctor, the nurse says: "They're on their way from resus. Keep going."
  • If they ask for IV furosemide (Lasix), the nurse gives it. Nothing changes within the station time.
  • If they do nothing for your breathing in the first few minutes, the nurse says: "His sats are down to 84% and his resp rate is 36." You become harder to understand.
  • If they ask for the X-ray or blood results now, the examiner says these will be given in Part 2.

Opening line: "I've been feeling... more and more short of breath... for the last 3 hours."

History (give only when asked; short phrases):

The breathlessness

  • Onset: it started about 2 weeks ago and has got steadily worse. In the last 3 hours it has become much worse.
  • Now: "I can't breathe properly." You are breathless even sitting still and struggle to finish a sentence.
  • Exertion: worse when you move. Over the 2 weeks you have not been able to walk as far as usual.
  • Lying flat: much worse lying down. You now sleep propped up on 3 pillows.
  • At night: you wake up gasping for air.

Other symptoms (only if asked)

  • Cough: for 2 weeks, getting worse. Only if asked what you are coughing up: frothy, pinkish sputum.
  • Tiredness: you have felt very tired.
  • Sweating and heart: you are sweaty and can feel your heart beating fast. It feels fast but regular.
  • Chest pain: no chest pain or tightness, nothing like your heart attack. No pain going to the arm, neck or jaw. No nausea. No sharp pain when you breathe in. Pain is not eased by leaning forward.
  • Infection: no fever or shivers, no yellow or green phlegm, no sick contacts, no recent cold or flu.
  • Lungs: no wheeze, no asthma, no emphysema or COPD that you know of. No sudden sharp pain at the start.
  • Clots: no calf pain or swelling, no recent operations, long trips or time in bed. No coughing up of pure blood.
  • Legs: you have not noticed your ankles swelling.
  • Bleeding and anaemia: no black or bloody stools, no vomiting blood, no unusual bruising.
  • Kidneys: perhaps passing a bit less urine over the last few days. No pain passing urine.
  • Injury: no falls or injury to the chest.
  • Fainting: none.

Past medical history

  • Heart attack 1 month ago. You were in hospital, had an angiogram and a stent, and went home on new tablets.
  • High blood pressure since your 50s, never well controlled. The last reading at your GP was 154/100.
  • No other heart, lung or kidney problems that you know of.

Medications (you take them every day)

  • Aspirin.
  • Clopidogrel.
  • A statin (atorvastatin).
  • Perindopril.
  • Metoprolol.
  • Over the counter (only if asked about other medicines or anything from the chemist or supermarket): you have been taking a lot of ibuprofen (Nurofen) for 2 weeks for lower back pain after a day in the garden. "Two tablets, three or four times a day. It's only Nurofen, it's not a real medicine."
  • No fluid tablets. No Viagra or similar (only if asked).

Allergies: none.

Family history: both parents have died. Your mother had breast cancer and died at 78. Your father died of a stroke at 90. You have two siblings, both well. High blood pressure runs in the family.

Social history

  • Smoking: 10 cigarettes a day for 15 years. You have been cutting down since the heart attack but still have a few a day.
  • Alcohol: rarely. No recreational drugs.
  • Home: you live with your wife and you have been coping well at home.
  • You eat healthily and walk occasionally.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you are frightened this is another heart attack, only a month after the last one. You had no idea the Nurofen could matter. You want to be able to breathe, and you want your wife, who is in the waiting room, kept informed.

If the candidate asks whether anything else is worrying you, say: "Is my heart giving out, doctor?"

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: sitting bolt upright, using his neck and shoulder muscles to breathe, speaking 3 or 4 words at a time. Sweaty. Dusky lips. Pink frothy sputum in a tissue. Weight 88 kg.
  • Vital signs: as the nurse reported.
  • Hands: cool and clammy, capillary refill 3 seconds. No clubbing. Nicotine staining on the right fingers. Small healed puncture mark at the right wrist (angiogram).
  • Pulse: regular, normal volume; 114/min before treatment, or about 104/min if GTN has been given.
  • Blood pressure: 212/112 before treatment, or about 160/90 if GTN has been given.
  • JVP: raised, 5 cm above the sternal angle with him sitting upright.
  • Praecordium: apex beat displaced to the 6th intercostal space, anterior axillary line. No heaves or thrills.
  • Heart sounds: first and second heart sounds with an added third heart sound (gallop rhythm). No murmurs. No pericardial rub.
  • Respiratory: trachea central. Expansion reduced at both bases. Dull to percussion at both bases, resonant above. Reduced breath sounds at both bases. Fine inspiratory crackles over both lungs, from the bases up to the mid zones. No wheeze, no bronchial breathing.
  • Abdomen: soft, non-tender. Liver not palpable. No pulsatile mass.
  • Back (if examined): tender lumbar paraspinal muscles, no midline bony tenderness.
  • Legs: trace pitting oedema at both ankles. Calves soft and non-tender. Foot pulses present.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Sam's identity and asks whether he is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin.

Recognises severe respiratory distress from the nurse's observations and acts before finishing the history: keeps him sitting upright, asks for oxygen with a stated target and calls the senior ED doctor. Then keeps questions short and closed.
check.d: Credit when oxygen with a target (92 to 96%) and senior help are requested within the first few minutes. No credit for oxygen without a target.

check.x: History
Characterises the breathlessness:
check.d: Credit when the time course and at least one other kid are elicited.

kids.x: Time course: started about 2 weeks ago, steadily worse, much worse in the last 3 hours
Severity now: breathless at rest, cannot finish sentences
Exertion: worse on exertion, cannot walk as far as before

check.x: Elicits orthopnoea (worse lying flat, sleeps on 3 pillows) and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (wakes gasping for air).
Asks about associated symptoms: cough for 2 weeks, increasing, with frothy pinkish sputum; fatigue; sweating; a fast, regular heartbeat.
check.d: Credit when the character of the sputum (frothy, pink) is asked about and elicited.

check.x: Asks about features of the differentials across at least three systems:
check.d: Credit when at least three systems are covered, including chest pain for ACS.

kids.x: Cardiac: chest pain, radiation, nausea (ACS); pleuritic or positional pain, recent viral illness (pericarditis or myocarditis); palpitations, fainting (arrhythmia)
Respiratory: fever, purulent sputum, sick contacts (pneumonia); wheeze, known COPD or asthma; sudden pleuritic pain (pneumothorax); calf swelling, immobility, haemoptysis (PE)
Haematological: black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, bruising (anaemia or bleeding on aspirin, clopidogrel and ibuprofen)
Renal, fluid and other: urine output, ankle swelling (right heart failure, renal causes); chest trauma

check.x: Takes the past medical history: heart attack 1 month ago (angiogram and stent), and hypertension since his 50s, poorly controlled (last 154/100).
check.d: Credit when the recent MI with stent and the poorly controlled hypertension are both elicited.

check.x: Takes the regular medication history: aspirin, clopidogrel, atorvastatin, perindopril and metoprolol, with adherence, and notes he takes no diuretic.
Asks specifically about over-the-counter medicines and elicits regular ibuprofen (Nurofen) at high doses for 2 weeks for lower back pain.
Asks about allergies: none.

Takes a social and family history: smoking quantified (10 a day for 15 years, about 7.5 pack-years, still smoking a few a day), alcohol rarely, no drugs, lives with his wife and coping; family history of hypertension.
check.d: Credit when smoking is quantified and his home situation is asked about.

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: fears another heart attack, did not know ibuprofen could matter, wants to breathe and his wife kept informed.
Examination
General inspection: upright posture, accessory muscle use, words per breath, sweating, cyanosis and the pink frothy sputum, with the nurse's observations.
Cardiovascular examination for heart failure:
check.d: Credit when the JVP is examined plus at least one of the other two kids.

kids.x: Pulse rate and rhythm, BP and peripheral perfusion (cool, clammy)
Displaced apex beat and a third heart sound, with no murmur or rub

check.x: Respiratory examination finding fine inspiratory crackles from both bases to the mid zones, with dullness and reduced breath sounds at both bases (effusions), a central trachea and no wheeze.
check.d: Credit when bilateral crackles and bibasal dullness are found.

check.x: Examines the legs for oedema and DVT: trace pitting oedema at both ankles, calves soft and non-tender.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: RR 32 to 34 and SpO2 87 to 86% on room air are in the red zone and worsening, calling for a rapid response (senior ED doctor at the bedside now); systolic BP above 200 is in the yellow zone; HR is white but tachycardic.
check.d: Credit when RR and SpO2 are named as red zone with immediate escalation.

check.x: Interprets the ECG as sinus tachycardia with the anterior Q waves and T inversion of his recent MI, unchanged from the discharge ECG, and no new ST elevation or depression.
Interprets the cardiac markers: NT-proBNP 8400 ng/L strongly supports acute heart failure; a single mildly raised troponin (41 ng/L) is myocardial injury and needs a repeat to exclude a new infarct.

Interprets the renal function as an acute kidney injury (creatinine 150, up from 95 a month ago), most likely from ibuprofen with perindopril, with potassium at the top of normal, needing monitoring during diuresis.
Interprets the venous gas as a mild metabolic acidosis with a raised lactate (hypoperfusion and work of breathing) and no hypercapnia, so the oxygen target is 92 to 96%.
Identifies the features of pulmonary oedema on the chest X-ray and notes the AP film limits judgement of heart size:
check.d: Credit when at least 2 features are named and pulmonary oedema is stated.

kids.x: Patchy bilateral perihilar airspace opacification (alveolar oedema)
Increased upper lobe vasculature (upper lobe diversion)
Indistinct, probably enlarged heart (cardiomegaly, hard to judge on an AP film)

check.x: Gives the diagnosis as acute pulmonary oedema from congestive heart failure, precipitated by the recent MI and NSAID use (with uncontrolled hypertension), justified by orthopnoea, PND, pink frothy sputum, raised JVP, S3, crackles, NT-proBNP and the X-ray.
Names differentials with a feature for or against each: recurrent MI or ACS, pneumonia, PE, COPD exacerbation and arrhythmia.
check.d: Credit when at least 3 differentials are named, including ACS, each with a feature from this patient.

check.x: Management
Escalates to the senior ED doctor and starts CPAP/NIV early for persisting distress or hypoxaemia, titrating oxygen to SpO2 92–96%.

Gives nitrates while systolic BP stays above 100 mmHg: sublingual GTN 300 to 600 microgram (or 400 microgram spray) repeated, then an IV GTN infusion titrated to symptoms and BP, after checking for recent PDE5 inhibitor use.
check.d: Credit for GTN with a stated systolic threshold of 90 to 100 mmHg; dose and PDE5 check are extra credit.

check.x: Gives IV furosemide 20 to 40 mg (diuretic-naive), with fluid balance and UEC/potassium monitoring.
check.d: Credit for IV furosemide plus monitoring of fluid balance and renal function or potassium.

check.x: Stops the ibuprofen and explains why: NSAIDs cause salt and water retention, worsen heart failure and kidney function, and raise bleeding risk with aspirin and clopidogrel.
States that routine morphine is not recommended in acute pulmonary oedema.
Plans repeat troponin and an echocardiogram, withholds perindopril while the creatinine is rising, and admits under cardiology (CCU).
Discharge medicines and safety netting

Names the medicines with a mortality benefit in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, mineralocorticoid antagonist such as spironolactone, SGLT2 inhibitor) and states that furosemide gives symptom relief only.
check.d: Credit when at least 3 are named with the furosemide point.

check.x: Tells Sam in plain words to call 000 after discharge for breathlessness at rest or lying flat, waking gasping, pink frothy sputum, chest pain, fainting or a racing heart.
Advises daily morning weights (see the GP if up more than 2 kg over 2 days) and no anti-inflammatories from the chemist, using paracetamol for his back instead.
Arranges GP review within 1 to 2 weeks and cardiology/heart failure program follow-up, with Quitline.

part2.lead: Here are his observations, the ECG the nurse recorded, his blood results with the venous gas, and the portable chest X-ray report.
part2.patient:
Ask these only after the examiner reads question 4, one at a time, still a little short of breath:

  • "Was it the Nurofen? It was only from the chemist."
  • "What can I take for my back then?"

You are relieved it is not a new heart attack so far. If the candidate explains clearly and kindly, you agree to stop the Nurofen and ask them to tell your wife. If they use jargon, ask what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Both sets on room air, before the medical review and before any treatment.
handover.model:
• Read (NSW Between the Flags adult observation chart): at triage RR 32 and SpO2 87% on room air are in the red zone; systolic BP 206 (above 200) is in the yellow zone; HR 108 and temperature 36.8 °C are white. At 10:50 RR 34 and SpO2 86% are still red and worse, HR has risen to 114 (white) and BP is 212/112 (yellow).
  • Meaning: severe, worsening respiratory failure with marked hypertension and tachycardia, afebrile: this fits hypertensive acute pulmonary oedema, not shock or sepsis. A white zone heart rate does not make him safe.
  • Changes: the red zone calls for a rapid response; in the ED that means the senior ED doctor at the bedside now, continuous monitoring, oxygen to 92 to 96%, early CPAP and nitrates while the BP is high. The yellow zone BP also calls for clinical review and is the target of the nitrates.

rows.note: Triage ATS 2: to acute bay, monitor on, ECG done
Repeat set on room air before medical review

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG of Mr Sam Stevens, DOB 14/03/1949, recorded at 10:46 today (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV).

  • Rate: 112/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus tachycardia. Regular, with a normal P wave before every QRS.
  • Axis: normal, about +30°.
  • PR interval: 170 ms.
  • QRS duration: 96 ms. No bundle branch block.
  • QTc: 430 ms (Bazett).
  • ST segments and T waves: no ST elevation in any lead. No ST depression. Shallow T wave inversion in V1 to V4.
  • Other: Q waves in V1 to V3 with poor R wave progression. No pathological Q waves in the inferior or lateral leads.
  • Comparison: the discharge ECG from his MI admission 4 weeks ago shows the same Q waves in V1 to V3 and T inversion in V1 to V4, in sinus rhythm at 62/min. The only change is the heart rate.
handover.model:
• Read: sinus tachycardia at 112/min, normal axis and intervals. Anterior Q waves with T inversion in V1 to V4, the same as the discharge ECG a month ago. No ST elevation or depression and no new change.
  • Meaning: the pattern of his recent anterior MI, with likely anterior wall damage and reduced pump function. No STEMI and no arrhythmia such as AF to explain the decompensation. An unchanged ECG does not exclude a new NSTEMI.
  • Changes: no reperfusion pathway; serial ECGs with a repeat troponin; treat the pulmonary oedema now.

handover.label: Bloods and venous blood gas
handover.result: Venous sample collected 10:45, about 3 hours after the breathlessness became much worse. Repeat troponin due.
handover.model:
• Read: NT-proBNP 8400 ng/L, far above the 900 ng/L rule-in level for his age. hs-troponin I 41 ng/L, just above the male 99th percentile of 34, a single value. Creatinine 150 (95 at discharge 4 weeks ago, about 1.6 times baseline) with eGFR 39 and urea 11.4; potassium 5.1 at the top of normal; sodium normal. Hb, WCC and platelets normal; CRP 9. Venous pH 7.30, normal pCO2, bicarbonate 21, base excess −4, lactate 2.8.
  • Meaning: strong support for acute heart failure. Myocardial injury is present, but one value cannot separate a new MI from strain on a failing heart a month after an infarct. An acute kidney injury, most likely from ibuprofen on top of perindopril. eGFR is not valid in AKI; follow the creatinine trend. No anaemia, no infection on the bloods. A mild lactic metabolic acidosis from hypoperfusion and the work of breathing, with no hypercapnia.
  • Changes: repeat troponin; oxygen target 92 to 96%; stop the ibuprofen; withhold perindopril while the creatinine is rising; daily UEC and potassium during diuresis.

rows.n: acute HF unlikely below 300; age 50-75 rule-in above 900

handover.label: Portable chest X-ray
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, portable AP erect. Mr Sam Stevens, DOB 14/03/1949, 20/04/2022, 11:00.

Clinical details: 73-year-old man with 2 weeks of worsening breathlessness, much worse over 3 hours, orthopnoea and PND. MI 1 month ago. SpO2 86% on room air.

Findings:

  • Technical: AP erect projection. Poor inspiration (patient breathless). Adequate exposure. Not significantly rotated.
  • Lines and devices: ECG electrodes.
  • Lungs: patchy airspace opacification throughout both lung fields, most marked in the perihilar regions, in keeping with alveolar oedema. Increased upper lobe vasculature (upper lobe venous diversion). No focal lobar consolidation. No pneumothorax.
  • Pleura: blunting of both costophrenic angles with meniscus-shaped opacity at both bases, in keeping with small to moderate bilateral pleural effusions.
  • Heart and mediastinum: the heart borders are indistinct. Heart size is difficult to assess on an AP film with poor inspiration but appears enlarged. Trachea central.
  • Bones and soft tissues: no acute bony abnormality.

Conclusion: appearances in keeping with acute pulmonary oedema, with small to moderate bilateral pleural effusions and probable cardiomegaly. Suggest repeat film after treatment.
handover.model:
• Read: checks the name, DOB and date; AP erect, poor inspiration, adequate exposure. Patchy bilateral perihilar airspace opacification (alveolar oedema, the 'bat wing' pattern), upper lobe diversion, blunted costophrenic angles (bilateral effusions), and an indistinct, probably enlarged heart that is hard to judge on an AP film. No pneumothorax, no lobar consolidation.
  • Meaning: acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, matching the crackles, bibasal dullness, raised JVP and S3. Of the ABCDE features, it shows alveolar oedema, cardiomegaly, dilated upper lobe vessels and effusions (Kerley B lines are not described). Bilateral, widespread change with effusions argues against a pneumonia.
  • Changes: treat as APO now; repeat the film after diuresis to check the oedema and effusions clear.

ask: You are now calling the cardiology registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Sam Stevens, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Sam now, here in the emergency department.
Before Sam goes home, what would you tell him about his medicines and the warning signs, and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, ED intern; Sam Stevens, 73.
  • Situation: acute pulmonary oedema; RR 34 and SpO2 86% on room air (red zone, worsening), BP 212/112, HR 114.
  • Background: 2 weeks worsening SOB, 3 h acute deterioration, orthopnoea, PND, pink frothy sputum; anterior MI with stent 1 month ago on DAPT, ACEi, beta-blocker; uncontrolled HTN; 2 weeks regular OTC ibuprofen; no allergies.
  • Assessment: raised JVP, S3, crackles to mid zones, bibasal dullness; ECG sinus tachycardia, old anterior Q waves, no new change; NT-proBNP 8400; troponin 41, single value; AKI (creatinine 150 from 95); lactate 2.8, no hypercapnia; CXR (AP, poor inspiration): alveolar oedema, upper lobe diversion, bilateral effusions, probable cardiomegaly.
  • Recommendation: Oxygen to 92–96%, CPAP being started by the ED team, GTN and IV furosemide given, ibuprofen stopped, perindopril withheld; please review for CCU admission under cardiology; repeat troponin due.

Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from congestive heart failure, precipitated by the recent MI and NSAID use (plus uncontrolled hypertension): orthopnoea, PND, pink frothy sputum; raised JVP, S3, crackles; NT-proBNP 8400; CXR oedema, upper lobe diversion, effusions.

  • Recurrent MI or ACS: for: MI a month ago, sweaty, troponin 41; against: no chest pain, ECG unchanged. Repeat troponin.
  • Pneumonia: for: 2 weeks of cough, patchy opacification; against: no fever, pink not purulent sputum, normal WCC, bilateral with effusions.
  • PE: for: hypoxia, tachycardia; against: no pleuritic pain or calf swelling, orthopnoea and PND, oedema on CXR.
  • COPD exacerbation or arrhythmia: against: no COPD or wheeze, no hypercapnia; ECG sinus rhythm.

1. Escalate and support breathing: senior ED doctor at the bedside; sit upright; titrate oxygen to SpO2 92 to 96%; start CPAP/NIV early for persisting distress or hypoxaemia; ICU if he fails.
  2. Nitrates: sublingual GTN 300 to 600 microgram (or 400 microgram spray) repeated, then IV GTN infusion titrated; keep systolic BP above 100; check PDE5 inhibitors.
  3. IV furosemide 20 to 40 mg (diuretic-naive), with fluid balance and UEC/potassium monitoring.
  4. Stop ibuprofen; withhold perindopril while the creatinine is rising.
  5. Morphine not routinely recommended.
  6. Repeat troponin and echo; admit to CCU under cardiology.

Model point, not scored: continue aspirin, clopidogrel and atorvastatin, and continue metoprolol unless hypotensive or shocked.

• Medicines: the Nurofen made his body hold fluid and strained his heart and kidneys; no anti-inflammatories (including from the chemist); paracetamol for his back. Continue aspirin and clopidogrel. Heart failure tablets that help him live longer (ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, spironolactone, SGLT2 inhibitor) will be adjusted once the echo is done; the fluid tablet is for symptoms only.
  • Red flags (000): breathless at rest or lying flat, waking gasping, pink frothy spit, chest pain, fainting, racing heart.
  • Daily weights: GP if up more than 2 kg over 2 days.
  • Follow-up: GP within 1 to 2 weeks; cardiology/heart failure program; Quitline.

ddx.dx: Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from congestive heart failure after a recent myocardial infarction, precipitated by NSAID use and uncontrolled hypertension
ddx.for: Two weeks of worsening breathlessness with orthopnoea, PND and pink frothy sputum a month after an MI, 2 weeks of regular ibuprofen, a raised JVP, S3 and crackles, NT-proBNP 8400 and a chest X-ray showing alveolar oedema, upper lobe diversion and effusions.
MI with a stent a month ago, sweating and a mildly raised troponin of 41 ng/L.
ddx.against: No chest pain, nausea or radiation, and the ECG is unchanged from his discharge ECG.

ddx.for: Acute worsening with hypoxia and tachycardia.
ddx.against: No pleuritic pain, calf swelling or immobility, and orthopnoea, PND, an S3 and oedema on X-ray explain the picture.

ddx.for: Two weeks of worsening cough with patchy opacification on the X-ray.
ddx.against: No fever or purulent sputum, normal WCC, only a small CRP rise, and the change is bilateral with upper lobe diversion and effusions.

ddx.dx: Exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
ddx.for: He is a current smoker with acute breathlessness.
ddx.against: Only about 7.5 pack-years, no known COPD, no wheeze and no hypercapnia on the venous gas.

ddx.dx: Tachyarrhythmia such as atrial fibrillation precipitating heart failure
ddx.for: He feels his heart beating fast a month after an MI.
ddx.against: The pulse is regular and the ECG shows sinus tachycardia.

guide:
In Part 1, the nurse gives the two room-air observation sets at the start. Sam is very breathless and answers in short phrases. A good candidate acts on the red zone observations (sits him up, oxygen with a target, senior help) before finishing the history, and that earns item 3. Give the ibuprofen only if the candidate asks about over-the-counter medicines or anything else he takes; a list of prescribed tablets alone does not reveal it. Give the pink frothy sputum only if the candidate asks what he is coughing up. Give examination findings only when the candidate says what they examine. If the candidate asks for the X-ray, ECG or bloods in Part 1, say they will be given in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over all four results, then ask the four questions in order. Sam asks his questions after question 4 is read. Continuing aspirin, clopidogrel, atorvastatin and metoprolol is a model point and is not scored.

A high-performing candidate characterises the 2-week course with the 3-hour deterioration, elicits orthopnoea, PND and the pink frothy sputum, and screens differentials across several systems, including bleeding on dual antiplatelets. They find the recent MI and the over-the-counter ibuprofen. They examine for a raised JVP, S3, crackles and effusions. In Part 2 they read the X-ray systematically, take the single raised troponin as needing a repeat, see the AKI, and give oxygen to target, CPAP, nitrates with a BP threshold and IV furosemide. They stop the ibuprofen, avoid routine morphine and know which drugs improve survival in heart failure.

A borderline candidate takes a generic breathlessness history, misses the ibuprofen or the orthopnoea, and does not examine the JVP. They may call the X-ray pneumonia, diagnose a new MI from the troponin alone, give oxygen without a target, or give routine morphine. Lying him flat, failing to escalate the red zone observations, or leaving the ibuprofen going is a serious safety concern.
explain:
Diagnosis: acute pulmonary oedema from congestive heart failure

Sam has acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (APO). His heart failure is most likely an ischaemic cardiomyopathy after his anterior MI a month ago. It decompensated because he took regular ibuprofen for 2 weeks on top of poorly controlled hypertension. NSAIDs cause sodium and water retention, raise blood pressure, blunt the effect of ACE inhibitors and diuretics, and can injure the kidneys, especially alongside an ACE inhibitor. His creatinine has risen from 95 to 150. With aspirin and clopidogrel, an NSAID also adds significant bleeding risk.

The history

  • Heart failure symptoms: exertional breathlessness and falling exercise tolerance, orthopnoea (how many pillows), PND, frothy pink sputum, fatigue, ankle swelling and weight gain.
  • Precipitants: ischaemia or reinfarction, arrhythmia (especially AF), uncontrolled hypertension, infection, non-adherence, salt or fluid excess, anaemia, renal impairment, and drugs that worsen heart failure: NSAIDs and glitazones (sodium and water retention), and verapamil or diltiazem (negative inotropy). Always ask about over-the-counter medicines.
  • Differentials across systems: cardiac (ACS, pericarditis or myocarditis, arrhythmia), respiratory (COPD, asthma, pneumonia, pneumothorax, PE), haematological (anaemia, which matters on dual antiplatelets with an NSAID), renal causes of fluid overload, and trauma.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: RR and SpO2 in the red zone and worsening call for a rapid response. Marked hypertension points to hypertensive APO, which responds well to nitrates.
  • ECG: sinus tachycardia with the anterior Q waves and T inversion of his recent MI, unchanged. No STEMI and no AF. An unchanged ECG does not exclude NSTEMI.
  • NT-proBNP: below 300 ng/L makes acute heart failure unlikely; above the age-related cut-off (900 ng/L at age 50 to 75) supports it.
  • Troponin: often raised in acute heart failure. A single raised value is myocardial injury; serial testing looks for the rise and fall of a new MI.
  • Renal function: creatinine 150 is about 1.6 times his baseline of 95, an AKI from NSAID plus ACE inhibitor, to be monitored during diuresis. Adding furosemide to an NSAID and ACE inhibitor completes the triple whammy, another reason to stop the ibuprofen and withhold the perindopril. eGFR is not valid in AKI; follow the creatinine trend.
  • Venous gas: lactic metabolic acidosis without hypercapnia, so the usual oxygen target applies.
  • Chest X-ray (ABCDE): Alveolar oedema (perihilar 'bat wing' opacification), B (Kerley B) lines, Cardiomegaly, Dilated upper lobe vessels, Effusions. Read the film systematically first: patient details, projection (AP films magnify the heart), inspiration and exposure.

Management

The traditional mnemonic is LMNOP, but current practice changes the order and drops routine morphine:

  1. Call for help, DRS ABCDE, continuous monitoring.
  2. Posture: sit upright.
  3. Oxygen only for hypoxaemia, titrated to SpO2 92 to 96% (TSANZ), weaning as he improves. Use CPAP or NIV for persisting respiratory distress or hypoxaemia: it reduces the work of breathing and the need for intubation.
  4. Nitrates reduce preload and afterload: sublingual GTN, then an IV infusion titrated to symptoms and BP, keeping systolic BP above 100 mmHg (avoid in hypotension, recent PDE5 inhibitor use, or significant aortic stenosis).
  5. Loop diuretic: IV furosemide (20 to 40 mg if diuretic-naive, more if already on a diuretic), with fluid balance, daily weights, renal function and potassium.
  6. Morphine appears in older teaching, but it is no longer recommended routinely. It is linked with more need for ventilation and worse outcomes.
  7. Stop the NSAID. Withhold the ACE inhibitor while the creatinine is rising. Continue the beta-blocker unless he is hypotensive or in shock. Continue dual antiplatelets and statin after a recent stent.
  8. Find the cause: repeat troponin and serial ECGs, and an echocardiogram for LV ejection fraction, wall motion and valves (including mitral regurgitation after MI).
  9. Disposition: admit to CCU under cardiology while on CPAP or a GTN infusion.

Long-term therapy

Furosemide relieves congestion but does not improve survival. In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, the medicines with a mortality benefit are an ACE inhibitor (or ARB, or sacubitril/valsartan), an evidence-based beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate CR or nebivolol), a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone or eplerenone) and an SGLT2 inhibitor (added in the 2022 Australian consensus update). They are started and up-titrated once he is stable, guided by the echo, renal function and potassium. If HFrEF is confirmed, his metoprolol tartrate should be changed to an evidence-based beta-blocker (e.g. metoprolol succinate CR or bisoprolol).

Safety netting and follow-up

Sam should avoid all NSAIDs, including those from the chemist and supermarket, and use paracetamol for his back. He should weigh himself every morning and see his GP if his weight rises by more than 2 kg over 2 days. He should call 000 for breathlessness at rest or lying flat, waking gasping, pink frothy sputum, chest pain, fainting or a racing heart. Follow-up includes his GP within 1 to 2 weeks, cardiology with the echo results, a heart failure management program, cardiac rehabilitation, blood pressure control and quit-smoking support.
points: Ask every breathless patient about orthopnoea (how many pillows), PND, frothy pink sputum and exercise tolerance, and examine the JVP, heart sounds for an S3, lung bases and ankles.
Always ask about over-the-counter medicines: NSAIDs cause fluid retention, worsen heart failure and kidney function, and add bleeding risk with dual antiplatelet therapy.
Read the chest X-ray systematically before the findings; the ABCDE of pulmonary oedema is alveolar oedema, Kerley B lines, cardiomegaly, dilated upper lobe vessels and effusions.
A raised NT-proBNP supports acute heart failure; a single raised troponin is myocardial injury and needs serial testing before a new MI is diagnosed.
Manage APO with the patient upright, oxygen titrated to SpO2 92 to 96%, early CPAP, nitrates while systolic BP stays above 100 mmHg and IV furosemide; morphine is not routinely recommended.
Furosemide relieves symptoms only; ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors improve survival in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
